title: Disaster recovery and multi-region
scopeHtml: Scope: RPO/RTO, DR strategies, active-passive vs active-active, replication and PITR, failover, drills, multi-region data.

notes.title: Disaster recovery basics: RPO and RTO
notes.html:
Disaster recovery (DR) is the plan to get a system working again after a big failure: a datacenter loss, region outage, data corruption, ransomware or a human mistake.

Two numbers define the plan:

  • RPO (Recovery Point Objective): how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RPO = 15 minutes means after recovery you may lose the last 15 minutes of writes. RPO = 0 means no loss, which needs synchronous replication.
  • RTO (Recovery Time Objective): how long you can be down. RTO = 1 hour means service restored within an hour.
        last good copy        disaster              service back
 ---------|---------------------|---------------------|--------->
          <------- RPO -------->|<-------- RTO ------->
          (data you lose)         (downtime you suffer)

Lower RPO and RTO cost more, roughly 10x per step. Business decides the numbers per system: a bank ledger might need RPO 0 and RTO minutes; an internal analytics dashboard can accept RPO 24 h and RTO 1 day.

Also distinguish:

  • High availability (HA): survive component failures automatically within a site/region (seconds to minutes).
  • DR: survive loss of the whole site or region, often with a human decision.
  • Backups: protect against corruption and deletion, which replication does NOT (it copies the bad delete everywhere).

Worked example. Payments service: RPO 0, RTO 5 min. Needs synchronous replication across zones (RPO 0 within region) plus a tested automatic failover. Reports service: RPO 24 h, RTO 8 h. A nightly snapshot copied to another region is enough, costing a few dollars per month.

Industry examples. AWS Well-Architected lists the four DR strategies (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active-active); Amazon S3 offers 11 nines of durability but customers still enable versioning because deletion by mistake is not covered by durability; GitLab's 2017 incident deleted production data and then found 4 of 5 backup methods were not working.

Everyday analogy. RPO is how many pages of your essay you can afford to lose if the laptop dies; RTO is how long you can go without a working computer before the deadline.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing RPO and RTO.
  • Saying replication replaces backups.
  • Setting RPO/RTO without discussing cost, or without business input.

notes.title: The four DR strategies
notes.html:
From cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest (the AWS framing):

Strategy RPO RTO Cost What runs in the DR region
Backup and restore Hours Hours to a day Lowest Nothing, only backups
Pilot light Minutes Tens of minutes Low Data replicated; core infra defined but off or minimal
Warm standby Seconds to minutes Minutes Medium Full stack at reduced capacity, running
Active-active (multi-site) Near 0 Near 0 (seconds) Highest Full stack serving real traffic

Backup and restore. Snapshots and WAL archives stored in another region. Recovery means creating infrastructure from code (Terraform) then restoring data; restore time depends on data size: 10 TB at 1 GB/s effective is still about 3 hours before verification.

Pilot light. Database replicated continuously; app servers exist as images/templates but are scaled to zero. On disaster scale them up and flip DNS.

Warm standby. A small but complete copy runs constantly (say 20% capacity). On failover autoscale to 100%. Fast, but must be validated: untested standby capacity limits cause failed failovers.

Worked example. Service costs 100K USD/month. Backup/restore adds about 2%, pilot light 10 to 15%, warm standby 30 to 50%, active-active 100%+ (plus complexity in data). Pick by the cost of downtime: if an hour of outage costs 500K USD, active-active may pay for itself with one avoided incident per year.

Decision gravity. The strategy is a business decision that shapes data architecture. Upgrading from pilot light to active-active later requires redesigning data replication and conflict handling: practically a one-way door, so decide the target early even if you start cheaper.

Industry examples. Netflix is active-active across AWS regions (evacuates a failing region in minutes using traffic steering); many banks use warm standby; startups usually start with backup/restore and cross-region snapshots.

Everyday analogy. Spare keys: one in a drawer at home (backup), a friend with a key and a bed made up (warm standby), or two flats you live in half the week (active-active).

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to active-active for everything.
  • Not accounting for data size when promising an RTO.
  • Forgetting that DR also needs secrets, DNS, certificates, and IAM in the second region.

notes.title: Active-passive vs active-active
notes.html:
Active-passive: one region serves traffic; the other is on standby and takes over on failure. Active-active: both (all) regions serve traffic at the same time.

Active-passive Active-active
Writes Single primary region Writes accepted in many regions
Failover Promote standby, flip traffic Remove failed region from routing
User latency Far users pay cross-region RTT Users hit the nearest region
Complexity Moderate High (conflicts, global uniqueness)
Wasted capacity Standby mostly idle None, but need headroom to absorb a lost region

The hard part is data. Active-active needs a strategy for concurrent writes:

  • Partition users by home region (geo-sharding): each user's data has one "home" write region; other regions only read or proxy. No conflicts, simple, but a failover moves ownership. Uber, Slack and many B2C apps do this.
  • Multi-leader replication with conflict resolution: LWW, CRDTs, application merge. DynamoDB global tables use last-writer-wins with timestamps; Cassandra multi-DC with LOCAL_QUORUM; CockroachDB/Spanner use consensus across regions (strong consistency, cross-region write latency of 50 to 150 ms).
  • Single write region, read replicas elsewhere: reads are local, writes pay the trip (Aurora Global Database: one writer region, replication typically under 1 second lag, cross-region failover/promotion takes about a minute in AWS docs; confirm).

Capacity math. With 2 active regions, to survive losing one, each must handle 100% of traffic: 2x provisioned, utilization capped at 50%. With 3 regions, each normally takes 1/3 of traffic; if one dies, each survivor takes 1/2, i.e. 1.5x its usual load, so each can run at up to 66% utilisation. More regions make N+1 cheaper.

Industry examples. Netflix (active-active, multi-region Cassandra); Amazon retail; Google Spanner (multi-region consensus); Facebook (regional with home-region data and TAO); Booking.com. DynamoDB global tables and Aurora Global DB are managed options.

Decision gravity. Active-passive is a modest, mostly reversible step. Active-active is a deep architectural commitment: you must design for it (idempotency, conflict handling, region-aware IDs). Adding it late is painful.

Everyday analogy. One shop open with a closed branch ready to open (active-passive), versus two branches both serving customers but needing to agree on stock numbers (active-active).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying active-active gives free availability. It brings conflict and consistency issues.
  • Forgetting the capacity math for losing a region.
  • Ignoring cross-region latency in synchronous replication.

notes.title: Replication, backups and point-in-time recovery
notes.html:
Replication keeps a live copy; backups keep history. You need both.

Replication modes:

  • Synchronous: the commit waits for the replica: RPO 0, but write latency includes the network RTT and availability depends on the replica. Cross-zone fine (1 to 2 ms), cross-region rarely (tens of ms per commit).
  • Asynchronous: the commit returns immediately; replica lags by milliseconds to seconds: RPO equals the lag at failure time (non-zero).
  • Semi-synchronous / quorum commit: at least one (or k of n) replica acks (Postgres synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (s1, s2)', MySQL semi-sync).
Postgres quorum commit (conceptual config)
synchronous_commit = on
synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (standby_az2, standby_az3)'
# Commit waits until any 1 standby has flushed WAL -> RPO ~0 inside the region, survives 1 standby loss

Point-in-time recovery (PITR). Take a base backup (e.g. daily) and continuously archive the write-ahead log (WAL) to object storage (S3). To recover to 10:42:17 (just before a bad DELETE), restore the base backup and replay WAL up to that time. RPO is about the WAL archive interval (seconds with streaming archive). Tools: pgBackRest, WAL-G, Barman for Postgres; AWS RDS automated backups (PITR with 5-minute granularity, retention up to 35 days; confirm current limits); MySQL binlogs.

Backup hygiene (3-2-1 rule). 3 copies, on 2 different media/systems, 1 offsite (another region or account). Protect backups from deletion: S3 Object Lock / immutable backups against ransomware, separate AWS account, versioning. Test restores regularly: an untested backup is a hope, not a backup.

Worked example. 2 TB Postgres, daily base backup (full ~2 TB compressed to ~600 GB) plus incremental WAL ~50 GB/day. Restore: download 600 GB at 500 MB/s is 20 minutes, replay 24 h of WAL at maybe 100 MB/s to 200 MB/s is under 10 minutes. RTO about 45 minutes before verification.

Real incident pattern. GitLab (Jan 31, 2017): an engineer removed the wrong database directory during replication troubleshooting; pg_dump backups were silently failing, S3 backup bucket empty, Azure disk snapshots not enabled for the DB; they recovered from a 6-hour-old LVM snapshot, losing about 6 hours of data. Lesson: monitor backup success, test restores.

Decision gravity. Retention length and immutability are reversible policy choices; the failure to test restores is the silent risk. Encryption key management for backups is a one-way door: lose the key and the backup is useless.

Industry examples. Amazon RDS/Aurora (continuous backup to S3), Google Cloud SQL PITR, Cloud Spanner backups, Etsy and GitHub with xtrabackup/replicas.

Everyday analogy. A video recording of your desk plus the photo album: the photo (base backup) plus a minute-by-minute diary (WAL) lets you reconstruct the desk at any moment.

Common interview traps.

  • Relying on replicas as backups.
  • Backups in the same account/region as the primary (one compromised account deletes both).
  • Not knowing how long a full restore takes.

notes.title: Failover: detection, promotion and traffic shifting
notes.html:
Failover is the sequence: detect failure, decide, promote the standby, redirect traffic, and fence the old primary.

Steps and timing (illustrative managed-DB numbers):

  1. Detect: health checks with consecutive failures (e.g. 3 x 10 s = 30 s). Faster detection raises false positives.
  2. Decide: automatic (needs reliable quorum/witness to avoid split brain) or manual (a human approves for region-level events, to avoid flapping).
  3. Promote: the replica becomes writable; check replication lag; for async you may lose the last transactions (RPO > 0).
  4. Redirect: DNS update (TTL 60 s but caches ignore it), global load balancer, or a service-discovery change. Connection pools must reconnect and applications must retry safely.
  5. Fence the old primary: make sure it cannot accept writes if it comes back (STONITH, read-only mode, revoke IAM), otherwise split brain.
  6. Rebuild redundancy: add a new standby.

Typical durations. Same-region Multi-AZ managed DB failover: 60 to 120 s (RDS docs commonly cite 1 to 2 minutes; Aurora often 30 s or less). Cross-region promotion: minutes plus DNS propagation. Kubernetes pod failure: seconds. Whole region evacuation with traffic steering: 1 to 10 min.

Traffic steering tools. DNS (Route 53 health-checked failover/latency records), global anycast load balancers (Cloudflare, Google Cloud Global LB, AWS Global Accelerator, which avoids DNS caching delays), service mesh locality failover (Envoy).

Worked example. 5,000 writes/s on async replication with 200 ms lag at failure: about 1,000 transactions (5,000 x 0.2) may be lost, which is the real RPO. Mitigation: semi-sync for critical tables, or reconcile from the application's event log/Kafka after failover.

Pitfalls.

  • Failback is harder than failover. Returning to the original region requires reverse replication and another cutover; plan it, and do not rush.
  • Control plane dependency: if your failover tool lives in the failed region, you cannot fail over. Keep the control plane independent (static stability: pre-provisioned capacity, no API calls needed during failure).
  • Thundering herd after failover: cold caches and connection storms overload the new primary; use warm-up and connection rate limits.

Industry examples. AWS "static stability" guidance; Facebook's Oct 2021 outage (BGP and DNS withdrawal made internal tools and even the data-centre access unreachable: control plane tied to the same network); Patroni/repmgr for Postgres HA; Orchestrator for MySQL; GitHub's 2018 incident from failover with split-brain-like divergence.

Decision gravity. Automatic vs manual failover: automatic is faster but can flap or split-brain on partial failures; many companies automate zone-level failover and keep region failover as a manual, rehearsed decision. Reversible by config.

Everyday analogy. A relief pilot: detect the captain is unwell, confirm, hand over controls, tell the tower, and make sure the original captain doesn't also grab the controls.

Common interview traps.

  • Ignoring failback and fencing.
  • DNS failover assuming clients honour the TTL.
  • A failover plan that depends on the very region that failed.

notes.title: Failover drills and game days
notes.html:
An untested DR plan almost always fails. Practice it on purpose.

Levels of practice:

  1. Tabletop exercise: talk through a scenario ("us-east-1 is gone, what do we do?") to find missing owners, runbooks, access.
  2. Restore test: regularly restore a backup into a scratch environment, run checksums/queries, record the actual duration (this becomes your measured RTO).
  3. Game day: controlled failure in production-like or production (kill a zone, block the primary) with observers and a stop button.
  4. Continuous chaos: automated random failure injection (Chaos Monkey; Netflix's Chaos Kong simulated whole-region loss).
  5. Regional evacuation drills: periodically run production traffic entirely from one region (Facebook's "storm" drills, Netflix regional failovers), proving capacity and tooling.

Checklist for a drill:

  • Define success: e.g. RTO 30 min, RPO 1 min, error rate below 1%.
  • Pre-announce, set blast-radius and abort criteria; have a rollback.
  • Verify with dashboards (SLO burn), not feelings.
  • Capture timeline, then fix gaps: missing IAM, expired certs, undersized standby, stale runbook, hardcoded IPs.
  • Re-run until boring.

Worked example. First drill: restore a 1.5 TB database. Expected RTO 1 h; actual 3 h 20 min because the restore role lacked KMS decrypt rights (45 min lost), the instance type was smaller than prod (1 h lost), and the runbook was outdated. Three fixes later, the second drill completes in 55 minutes.

Industry examples. Netflix Chaos Monkey/Kong; Google DiRT (Disaster Recovery Testing) exercises; AWS Fault Injection Service; Amazon "GameDay" tradition; Gremlin; GitHub and Stripe run regular failover tests.

Decision gravity. Drills cost engineering time and carry small risk but are cheap compared to a real failure; making them routine (quarterly) is a cultural choice. Fully reversible.

Everyday analogy. Fire drills: you find out the exit is blocked while the building is not on fire.

Common interview traps.

  • Documenting an RTO that was never measured.
  • Running drills only in staging that differs from prod.
  • Drills with no abort condition or no learning follow-up.

notes.title: Multi-region data and consistency trade-offs
notes.html:
Distance costs time: light in fibre travels about 200 km per ms, so a US-East to EU-West round trip is about 70 to 80 ms in practice, and to Asia 150 to 250 ms. That is a floor you cannot engineer away.

Options when a write must be durable in two regions:

  • Synchronous cross-region commit: adds one RTT to every write (e.g. +80 ms). Spanner/CockroachDB do this for strong consistency in multi-region mode, with tricks like placing the leaseholder near the users.
  • Async replication: fast writes, but non-zero RPO and eventual consistency across regions.
  • Per-user home region: pick the region where each user's data lives; most requests are local and fast; only cross-region requests pay.

Consistency patterns:

  • Read-your-writes: after a user writes, route their next reads to the same region (session stickiness, or read from primary for N seconds).
  • Global unique IDs: include a region code or use Snowflake-style IDs; do not rely on auto-increment across regions.
  • Idempotent event processing: replicate events through Kafka MirrorMaker/Cluster Linking and make consumers idempotent because duplicates and reordering appear around failover.
  • Global tables/secondary indexes: accept eventual consistency and design the UI for it.

Data residency. GDPR and country laws can require that some data stays in a region. This favors geo-sharding and shapes DR (backups can only go to allowed regions).

Cost. Cross-region data transfer costs money (on AWS roughly 0.02 USD/GB between regions; confirm current price). Replicating 20 TB/month is about 400 USD, but chatty cross-region service calls can silently add up.

Worked example. Chat app with 50M users across US/EU/Asia. Messages are stored in the sender's home region and replicated asynchronously to the recipient's region; delivery adds typically 100 to 300 ms inter-region latency, acceptable. Account creation uses a globally unique handle check: a rare strongly consistent global operation, done synchronously in a single "directory" region.

Industry examples. WhatsApp and Slack use regional/cell designs; Discord and Instagram use geo-aware routing; CockroachDB REGIONAL BY ROW; DynamoDB global tables; Cosmos DB multi-region with tunable consistency levels.

Decision gravity. Where each piece of data lives (home region, global, replicated) is a one-way door: re-homing data later is a migration project. Decide what MUST be strongly consistent globally (usernames, payments, inventory) and keep that set tiny.

Everyday analogy. Letters between cities: you can wait for confirmation of receipt every time (slow, certain), or send many and reconcile later (fast, occasionally confused).

Common interview traps.

  • Pretending cross-region synchronous replication is free.
  • Auto-increment IDs in multiple active regions.
  • Forgetting data residency law.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• RPO = data loss tolerance, RTO = downtime tolerance; each step lower costs roughly 10x. HA is not DR is not backup.
  • Four strategies: backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active; choose by business cost of downtime; moving to active-active later is a one-way door.
  • Active-active needs a data plan: home-region sharding, multi-leader conflict resolution, or cross-region consensus (Spanner, CockroachDB). Capacity must cover a lost region.
  • Replication (sync/async/quorum) does not replace backups; use PITR (base backup plus WAL), 3-2-1, immutable and offsite copies, and test restores (GitLab 2017).
  • Failover: detect, decide, promote, redirect, fence; failback is harder; keep the control plane independent of the failed region.
  • Drill regularly (tabletop, restore tests, game days, chaos); measure real RTO/RPO.
  • Cross-region latency (about 70 to 250 ms) is physics; keep strongly consistent global data minimal.

questions.promptHtml: Define RPO and RTO, and explain how high availability, disaster recovery and backups differ.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates often mix the terms and claim replication replaces backups.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: RPO is how much data I can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO is how long I can be down. HA survives component failures inside a site automatically; DR survives loss of a whole site or region, often with a human decision; backups protect against corruption and deletion, which replication does not because it copies the bad delete everywhere. Business sets the numbers, and each step lower costs roughly 10x.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
last good copy        disaster              service back
 ---------|---------------------|---------------------|--------->
          <------- RPO -------->|<-------- RTO ------->
          (data you lose)         (downtime you suffer)

RPO 0 needs synchronous replication. A payments ledger might need RPO 0 and RTO 5 minutes; an internal dashboard can accept RPO 24 h and RTO 1 day, served by a nightly cross-region snapshot costing a few dollars per month. Replication is not backup: DELETE FROM orders replicates in milliseconds. Durability (S3 11 nines) does not cover accidental deletion, so people enable versioning.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Swapping RPO and RTO.
  • "We have replicas, so backups are redundant."
  • Choosing numbers without cost or business input.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Who sets RPO/RTO? -> Business, from the cost of downtime and data loss, per system.
  2. How do you prove RTO? -> Restore drills that measure real time, not estimates.
  3. What did GitLab 2017 teach? -> A deletion with 4 of 5 backup methods not working; test restores and monitor backup jobs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: defines the acronyms. Senior: ties them to cost, separates HA/DR/backup, and insists on measured numbers.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team with 3 replicas lost a table to a faulty migration because nobody could restore to a point in time.

questions.promptHtml: Compare backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and active-active. How do you pick?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks cost-aware judgement rather than "always active-active".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: From cheap and slow to expensive and fast: backup and restore (hours of RPO and RTO, nothing running), pilot light (data replicated, core infrastructure defined but off), warm standby (full stack at reduced capacity running), active-active (full stack serving traffic, near zero RPO and RTO). I pick by the business cost of downtime against the extra cost, roughly 2%, 10 to 15%, 30 to 50% and 100%+ of the primary's bill.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Strategy RPO RTO Runs in DR region
Backup and restore Hours Hours to a day Nothing
Pilot light Minutes Tens of minutes Data replicated, infra minimal
Warm standby Seconds to minutes Minutes Full stack, small
Active-active Near 0 Near 0 Full stack, live
Restore time is bounded by data size: 10 TB at 1 GB/s is about 3 hours before verification. If an hour of outage costs 500K USD, active-active (100K USD/month extra on a 100K system) pays for itself with one avoided incident per year.
Moving from pilot light to active-active later means redesigning data replication and conflict handling: a one-way door, so decide the target early.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Active-active for everything.
  • Promising an RTO without counting data size.
  • Forgetting secrets, DNS, certificates and IAM in the second region.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Warm standby risk? -> Untested capacity; scale-up may hit quota or fail.
  2. Pilot light first step in a disaster? -> Scale app tiers from images, promote the replica, flip DNS.
  3. How to start cheap but not paint into a corner? -> Region-aware IDs and idempotent events from day one.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: lists the four. Senior: ties each to cost, data size and irreversible architecture choices.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A startup promised RTO 15 minutes with backup/restore; the first real restore of 6 TB took 9 hours.

questions.promptHtml: What makes active-active hard, and how do you handle writes and capacity?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The difficulty is data, not routing; seniors know the options.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Routing is easy; concurrent writes are hard. I choose among partitioning users by home region (no conflicts, simple, failover moves ownership), multi-leader replication with conflict resolution (LWW, CRDTs, app merge), or cross-region consensus (Spanner, CockroachDB, paying 50 to 150 ms per write). Capacity: with 2 regions each must hold 100% so run at 50% utilisation; with 3 regions each takes 50% on loss, so about 66% utilisation.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Users EU -> Region EU -> (EU database)
Users US -> Region US -> (US database)

Single write region with read replicas elsewhere (Aurora Global style): local reads, writes pay the trip, cross-region promotion takes about a minute (verify). DynamoDB global tables use last-writer-wins. IDs must be region-aware or Snowflake-style, not auto-increment. Capacity formula: N regions, lose one, survivors take N/(N-1) of their normal load: 2 regions 2x, 3 regions 1.5x, 4 regions 1.33x.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Active-active gives free availability."
  • Forgetting the lost-region capacity math.
  • Ignoring cross-region latency in synchronous replication.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is LWW dangerous? -> Clock skew silently drops a valid write; bad for money or counters.
  2. How do you handle a global unique username? -> A small strongly consistent global directory service.
  3. Read-your-writes? -> Sticky session to the home region or read from primary for N seconds.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "two regions behind a global load balancer". Senior: picks a data model, shows capacity math and names the consistency boundary.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team using auto-increment IDs in two active regions hit duplicate keys at the first cross-region sync.

questions.promptHtml: Explain synchronous, asynchronous and quorum replication, and how point-in-time recovery works.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests RPO reasoning and whether you can recover from a human error.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Synchronous commit waits for the replica: RPO 0 but write latency includes the RTT and availability depends on the replica. Asynchronous returns immediately: faster but RPO equals the lag at failure. Quorum commit waits for any k of n replicas. PITR is a periodic base backup plus continuously archived write-ahead log; I restore the base and replay the log to just before the mistake.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
synchronous_commit = on
synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (standby_az2, standby_az3)'
# commit waits until any 1 standby flushed WAL: RPO ~0 in region, survives loss of 1 standby

Cross-zone sync costs 1 to 2 ms; cross-region tens of ms per commit. PITR tools: pgBackRest, WAL-G, Barman; RDS automated backups allow 5-minute granularity with retention up to 35 days (verify current limits). Worked restore: 2 TB database, base compressed to 600 GB; download at 500 MB/s is 20 minutes; replay 24 h of WAL in under 10 minutes; RTO about 45 minutes before verification. 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 offsite; immutable (Object Lock) and in a separate account; losing the encryption key makes the backup useless.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using replicas as backups.
  • Backups in the same account and region as the primary.
  • Never timing a full restore.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a separate account? -> One compromised credential should not delete primary and backups.
  2. How to recover a single dropped table? -> Restore to a scratch instance at the earlier time and copy the table back.
  3. How do you monitor backups? -> Alert on missing WAL segments and failed jobs, and run automated restore tests.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "replicas and nightly backups". Senior: ties replication mode to RPO, builds PITR, immutability, key management and restore tests.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: GitLab 2017: pg_dump silently failing, empty S3 bucket, recovery from a 6-hour-old snapshot.

questions.contextHtml: At 10:43:05 an engineer runs DELETE FROM payments WHERE status = 'pending' against production without a WHERE on the right environment filter, removing 1.2M rows. Three read replicas applied it within 200 ms. The database is Postgres 15, 2 TB, with pgBackRest: nightly base backup at 02:00 (about 600 GB compressed) and WAL archived to S3 every 60 s. Restore throughput from S3 is 500 MB/s and WAL replay about 100 MB/s; 24 h of WAL is about 50 GB. The system is still serving other tables.
questions.promptHtml: Walk through recovery, with the time estimate and what you would not do.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Fail over to a replica." The replicas already have the delete.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Exact time of the delete (from logs)? Are other writes since then valuable? Can the app tolerate payments being read-only? Is a recent logical backup available?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop writes to the payments table (revoke or app flag), keep other tables running; take a snapshot of the current state; stop replicas from being promoted.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) PITR to 10:43:04 on a scratch instance, then copy the rows back; (b) full-database PITR (more downtime, loses later legit writes); (c) logical recovery from audit logs if exists.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check WAL archive continuity (pgbackrest info), test restore on a scratch host with --type=time --target='2025-... 10:43:04' (set the right time zone).
  5. Root cause: Human error with insufficient guard rails; replication copied it.
  6. Fix: Restore the base (600 GB at 500 MB/s is 20 minutes) and replay about 8.7 h of WAL (about 18 GB at 100 MB/s is 3 minutes plus overhead), total roughly 30 to 45 minutes; verify row counts; copy missing rows with INSERT ... SELECT via a foreign table or dump; reconcile later payments.
pgbackrest --stanza=main --type=time \
  --target="2025-03-14 10:43:04+00" --target-action=promote restore
  1. Prevention: Require a transaction and a row-count check for manual DML, read-only default roles, delayed replica (for example 1 hour) as quick recovery, restore drills.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not restore over production; not promote a replica; not guess the timestamp without checking the timezone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• WAL archive has a gap? -> Recovery stops at the gap; that is why you alert on archive failures.
  • Delayed replica? -> A 1-hour lag replica lets you pause replay before the delete and copy back in minutes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team recovered in 40 minutes because they had practised monthly; another needed 6 hours because the restore role lacked KMS rights.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fail over.
  • Hire: PITR to scratch instance and copy back.
  • Strong hire: contains blast radius, does time math, checks WAL continuity and adds guard rails and a delayed replica.

questions.contextHtml: An orders database in region A has an async replica in region B. Writes are 5,000 per second; replication lag shows 200 ms normally and 3 s at peak. Region A fails at 14:00:00 with a power event. The team promotes region B at 14:07. After promotion the business reports 14,000 missing orders. The runbook says RPO = 0 because "we have a replica". A manager asks whether the data is recoverable.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the loss, what you do now, and how you would redesign.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replication should be zero loss." Confuses async with sync.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was replication async? What was the lag at failure? Is there an outbox, Kafka log or payment provider records with these orders? Did the old primary's disk survive?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep region B as the single writer; fence region A; announce the data gap and freeze reconciling writes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Expected loss: 5,000 x 3 s = 15,000 orders at peak (14,000 matches); at normal lag 5,000 x 0.2 = 1,000. Real RPO = lag at failure, not zero.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare last applied LSN/binlog position on B with checkpoints; check event stream and payment provider settlement for orders missing in B.
  5. Root cause: An RPO target of 0 with an asynchronous mechanism.
  6. Fix: Recovery: rebuild missing orders from the event log (Kafka/outbox) and payment provider records; if A's disk can be recovered, extract its last WAL. Redesign: synchronous or quorum commit inside the region (RPO about 0 for node loss), and for cross-region either accept RPO of seconds (and say so) or use consensus storage with higher write latency (+70 to 80 ms) for the orders table only.
  7. Prevention: Alert on replication lag against the RPO; failover runbook that reports the expected data loss before promotion; idempotent order replays.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Cross-region sync costs about 80 ms per commit and couples availability to the remote region; keep it for tables that need it. Do not write "RPO 0" without a mechanism.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Business insists on RPO 0 across regions? -> Consensus database (Spanner/CockroachDB style) and accept latency and cost.
  • Customers charged but orders missing? -> Reconcile from the payment provider and re-create orders idempotently.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The runbook said RPO 0 for years; the first real failover revealed a 90-second effective RPO nobody had measured.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: assumes zero loss.
  • Hire: lag x rate explains the loss and proposes reconciliation.
  • Strong hire: restates RPO honestly, designs per-table sync policy and alerts on lag.

questions.contextHtml: A SaaS company with 100K USD per month infrastructure has three systems: a customer-facing API (an hour of downtime costs about 80K USD revenue and trust), an internal analytics warehouse (8 TB, used by analysts) and a billing batch system (runs nightly, a missed run delays invoices by a day). The CFO says "make everything survive a region loss, budget is 40K USD per month extra." Current DR: nightly snapshots in the same region.
questions.promptHtml: Assign DR strategies, with RPO/RTO and rough costs, and defend the plan.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Active-active for all three." Blows the budget and ignores restore math.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Business RPO/RTO per system? Regulatory data location limits? How fast does data change? Who decides on region failover?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move snapshots to another region and another account now (cheap, big gain).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: API: warm standby (30 to 50% of its share) for RTO in minutes, RPO seconds. Analytics: backup and restore cross-region; 8 TB at 1 GB/s is about 2.5 hours plus verification, acceptable for RTO 8 h. Billing: pilot light or just restore, since a day's delay is tolerable and it runs nightly.
  4. How I'd verify each: Restore test timings; cost model per strategy; load test the warm standby at 100% scale-up.
  5. Root cause: Without differentiated targets, a single "survive everything" requirement is either unaffordable or untested.
  6. Fix: API warm standby with async cross-region database replica; promoted via a rehearsed manual decision for region events; analytics with weekly full and daily incremental to another region; billing with infrastructure as code that can be recreated and the data replicated. Total roughly: API 25K, analytics 3K, billing 4K, about 32K USD per month, under budget.
  7. Prevention: Quarterly drills measure actual RTO; keep secrets, DNS, IAM and certificates in the DR region.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Active-active for the API would cost 100%+ and need conflict handling; revisit only if downtime cost justifies. Upgrading later is a one-way door, so keep IDs region-aware now.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Downtime cost rises to 500K USD per hour? -> Reconsider active-active for the API.
  • Data residency forbids a second region? -> A second zone set within the country, and backups only to allowed regions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A company found its pilot-light region had no quota for the instance type it needed; the "20 minute" failover took 3 hours of support tickets.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: everything active-active.
  • Hire: tiered strategies with RPO/RTO and rough cost.
  • Strong hire: restore-time math, budget fit, drills and the one-way-door note.

questions.contextHtml: A Postgres primary in zone A loses connectivity to the monitor for 40 s because of a network partition, though it still serves some app servers. The automatic failover (health check 3 failures x 10 s) promotes the standby in zone B. For 6 minutes both nodes accept writes: 2,300 orders on A and 1,900 on B, with overlapping order numbers (sequences). After the network heals, replication cannot resume (timelines diverged). Customers see missing and duplicate orders.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong and how do you recover and prevent a repeat?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the health check faster." That raises false positives and still doesn't fence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a witness or quorum? Was the old primary fenced (STONITH, network, IAM)? How do apps discover the primary (DNS, config)? What identifiers collide?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop writes on one node: make A read-only/shut down; choose the surviving timeline (B or A) based on which has more valuable data; freeze order creation if needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) no fencing of the old primary; (b) a monitor partition treated as primary failure; (c) clients still pointing at A through cached DNS or connection pools; (d) sequences without a region or node prefix.
  4. How I'd verify each: Timeline IDs, pg_controldata, WAL positions, application logs per node, and the failover tool's decision log.
  5. Root cause: Split brain: the decision logic lacked quorum and the old primary was not prevented from accepting writes.
  6. Fix: Recovery: pick the winner, rebuild the other with pg_rewind or fresh base backup, export the divergent orders from the loser and re-insert with new IDs after business reconciliation. Prevention: failover via a consensus store (Patroni with etcd/Consul) using leader leases so the old primary demotes itself when it loses the lease; fencing (power or network or revoking storage); route clients through a proxy that only the leader owns.
  7. Prevention: Failover game days with partition injection; monitor timeline divergence; automatic failover only at zone level and manual at region level.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Faster detection increases false positives and flapping; slower detection increases downtime. Not "just pick the one with more rows" without business reconciliation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does synchronous replication prevent this? -> It reduces data divergence, but without fencing a partitioned old primary may still accept local writes (they just won't commit if sync is required).
  • Multi-AZ managed DB? -> The vendor implements the fencing; still test application reconnection.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A manual "quick failover" without fencing left a forgotten cron job writing to the old primary for two days.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: faster health checks.
  • Hire: identifies fencing and split brain, reconciles data.
  • Strong hire: lease-based leadership, partition game days and a reconciliation plan with business input.

questions.contextHtml: The first-ever restore drill of a 1.5 TB production database. The documented RTO is 1 hour. Timeline: 00:00 start; 00:20 the restore role cannot read the KMS key (45 minutes lost granting access); 01:05 download begins on an instance type with 2x less network and disk than production (restore takes 1 h 10 min); 02:15 starting the database fails because max_connections and a parameter group differ from production; 03:05 a runbook step references a retired bastion host; 03:20 the database is up and checks pass. The drill ran in staging, not the DR region.
questions.promptHtml: What do you conclude and what changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "RTO was 3h20, so update the document." Misses that the drill should be repeated until boring.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which steps are human latency vs machine time? What are the true dependencies (keys, networks, DNS, certificates)? Is the DR region able to do this at all?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Record the actual RTO as 3 h 20 min; tell the business the current exposure; fix the high-impact gaps first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Gaps: access (KMS/IAM), sizing (instance type), configuration drift (parameter group), stale runbook, wrong environment.
  4. How I'd verify each: Re-run the drill monthly with a timer and observers; compare time per step; automate with code.
  5. Root cause: RTO was a belief, never measured; DR environment configuration was not code.
  6. Fix: Infrastructure as code for the restore environment including IAM, KMS, parameter groups; restore automation script; runbook updated and executable; run in the actual DR region. Target second drill about 55 minutes; track steps.
# nightly automation sketch: restore latest backup to a scratch instance and run checks
pgbackrest --stanza=main --type=default --delta restore
psql -c "SELECT count(*) FROM payments" ; psql -f verify.sql
  1. Prevention: Quarterly game days; continuous restore verification; checklist for new data stores to include DR; alert if the last successful restore test is older than 30 days.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Drills consume engineering time and carry small risk; they are cheap compared to a real failure. Not "fixing" the RTO by editing the doc.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Management wants a one-hour RTO now? -> Pilot light with a replica gives minutes for the data portion; a restore of 1.5 TB cannot be faster than the pipe.
  • What measure defines "done"? -> Two consecutive drills under target with no manual heroics.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's second drill took 52 minutes; a month later a real incident closed in 58.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: edits the doc.
  • Hire: lists gaps and fixes each.
  • Strong hire: automates, runs in the DR region, measures steps and sets repeat cadence.

questions.contextHtml: Product wants a chat app for 50M users in the US, EU and Asia: "messages should feel instant everywhere, nothing lost, usernames unique globally, and EU data must stay in the EU." Round-trip times: US-EU about 80 ms, US-Asia about 180 ms. The team proposes one globally replicated SQL database with synchronous replication.
questions.promptHtml: Ask clarifying questions, then design the data layer.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Synchronous global replication is fine." Adds 80 to 180 ms to every write and violates residency.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "instant" mean (p99 delivery under 300 ms)? Can message loss be tolerated for seconds (RPO)? Are chats cross-region often? Which law applies to EU data (GDPR) and what counts as personal data? What happens if a region is down?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed (design); but stop the global sync proposal.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Options: (a) global sync consensus (every write +80 to 180 ms, fails residency for replicated data), (b) per-user home region with async replication to recipients' regions, (c) multi-leader with LWW (risk of lost edits).
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype latency tests; confirm with legal what data may leave the region; model cross-region message share.
  5. Root cause (of the bad idea): Ignoring physics (light in fibre about 200 km/ms) and law.
  6. Fix: Home region per user; messages stored in the sender's region and delivered to the recipient's region asynchronously (typically 100 to 300 ms extra for cross-region), idempotent consumers and dedupe keys because duplicates and reordering appear near failover; a small strongly consistent global directory service in a single region for username uniqueness (rare operation); region-aware IDs (Snowflake-style); EU data stored only in EU, only pointers or anonymised metadata leave; read-your-writes via home-region stickiness. Cross-region transfer cost about 0.02 USD/GB (verify): 20 TB/month is about 400 USD.
  7. Prevention: Region failure drills; alerts on replication lag per region pair; audit of residency.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Home-region sharding makes failover move ownership and complicates travel users; global tables with LWW risk silent overwrites. Moving data between regions later is a migration project (one-way door).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• EU user messages a US user? -> Message copy delivered under legal basis; keep policy decisions explicit with legal.
  • Home region fails? -> Promote a replica in a paired in-law region for that cohort, or degrade to read-only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch with auto-increment IDs in two regions hit duplicate message IDs on the first cross-region sync.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: global sync DB.
  • Hire: home-region design with async replication and a small global directory.
  • Strong hire: asks about requirements and law, does latency and cost math, handles dedupe and failover ownership.

questions.contextHtml: An active-active service runs in 2 regions, each at 60% CPU at peak with 100 pods (4 vCPU each), total traffic 40,000 req/s. During a drill, region 2 was removed and region 1 hit 100% CPU, p99 went from 80 ms to 3.4 s and 35% of requests failed. Autoscaling reached its limit of 150 pods after 12 minutes. The CFO asks whether adding a third region would be cheaper than raising utilisation headroom.
questions.promptHtml: Do the capacity math and recommend options.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the autoscaler limit." Autoscaling is minutes slow and quotas may bind.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the autoscaler limit a quota or a cost cap? How fast is scale-up (cold start, image pull)? Can load be shed during a region loss? Does each region have independent dependencies (DB)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pre-warm capacity; raise quotas; add shedding by criticality for the failover window.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Two regions at 60% means one carries 120% of its capacity when the other dies: overload. To survive loss each region must run at no more than 50% (2 regions). Three regions: each normally 1/3; on loss each takes 1/2 (1.5x), so utilisation up to 66% is OK. Four regions: 1.33x, up to 75%.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per-pod capacity from load tests (requests per pod at p99 SLO); compute N+1 target; check DB and cache headroom, not just pods.
  5. Root cause: Utilisation target (60%) inconsistent with N+1 for 2 regions; reliance on autoscaling that is too slow.
  6. Fix: Option A: 2 regions at 50% = 120 pods each to carry 40k (current 100 pods at 60% implies 1 pod serves about 333 req/s at 60% peak; 40k total needs about 80 pods at 100% per region, i.e. 160 pods in a region to serve 100% at 50% headroom... use measured values). Option B: 3 regions at 66% target: total capacity needed = 40k / (2/3 of 3) ... roughly 120 pods each normal at 66%, cheaper in total than 2 x 160, at the cost of a third region's fixed overhead (data replication, ops). Compare: 2 regions: 2 x 160 = 320 pod; 3 regions: 3 x 107 = 321... (verify with measured per-pod capacity; the savings come mainly at 4+ regions or when fixed overhead is small).
  7. Prevention: Regular region-evacuation drills; capacity model in code; alert when headroom falls below N+1.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More regions raise data replication and operational complexity; do not choose a third region only for cost. Static headroom costs money but works instantly; autoscaling is cheaper but slow.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can load shedding replace headroom? -> Partly: shed non-critical traffic for 10 to 15 minutes while scaling.
  • DB capacity in the surviving region? -> Often the real limit; test it too.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The drill proved the stack survived region loss only at 40% of traffic; headroom was the missing feature, not code.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raise the autoscaler limit.
  • Hire: N/(N-1) math and the 50% rule.
  • Strong hire: compares 2 vs 3 regions with measured per-pod capacity, includes DB and shedding, and proposes drills.

questions.contextHtml: Region A suffers a network failure at 03:10. The runbook says: use the deployment tool (hosted in region A) to scale up region B, then update Route 53 records (TTL 60 s). The deployment tool is unreachable; engineers lose 25 minutes finding credentials in a secrets manager that also lives in region A. When DNS finally changes at 03:41, about 20% of mobile and corporate clients keep hitting A for another 15 minutes. Region B scales from 20% to 100% at 03:55 and its database falls over from a cold cache and 3x connection spike. RTO target was 15 minutes; actual was 58.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review and propose the redesign.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Lower the DNS TTL to 5 seconds." Addresses one of four problems.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What systems does failover depend on? Who can approve a region failover? Is capacity in B pre-provisioned? What did clients do with DNS?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Done during the incident: manual DNS change; going forward, steps for fast recovery should not need region A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) control plane tied to the failed region (deployment tool, secrets); (b) DNS caching beyond TTL; (c) no pre-provisioned capacity (scale-up at failure time); (d) cold cache and connection storm; (e) unclear decision authority (time lost).
  4. How I'd verify each: Timeline of each delay; dependency map of the runbook; DNS resolver tests; DB connection and cache metrics.
  5. Root cause: The failover depended on the failed region and on slow, uncontrolled mechanisms; static stability was missing.
  6. Fix: Static stability: pre-provision B at warm-standby capacity (so no API calls to scale during failure); control plane and secrets replicated and independent of A; traffic steering via anycast or a global load balancer (AWS Global Accelerator, Cloudflare, Google Global LB) rather than DNS alone; pre-warmed caches and connection-rate limits in B; a pre-authorised decision rule (for example 5 minutes of failing health checks equals go).
  7. Prevention: Quarterly region evacuation drill; runbook tests with region A blocked; alert on drift of the standby config.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Warm standby costs 30 to 50% extra; automatic region failover risks flapping, so keep the decision manual but pre-authorised. Not rely on "TTL is 60 s".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• How do you fail back? -> Reverse replication, drill it, move traffic gradually; failback is harder than failover.
  • What if B's DB cannot take the load? -> Rate-limit connections, warm cache, and shed non-critical traffic first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Facebook's 2021 outage is the famous version: internal tools depended on the network that failed, so recovery tooling was unreachable.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lower TTL.
  • Hire: spots the control-plane dependency and standby capacity.
  • Strong hire: designs static stability, traffic steering beyond DNS, warm-up and decision authority and tests with region A blocked.
